Yes. The clean derivation is:

[
u_0
\longrightarrow
\text{one pressure-complete NS history}
\longrightarrow
\text{its complete mixed derivative jet}
\longrightarrow
\text{all finite compatible rectangles}
\longrightarrow
\mathcal I[u_0]
]

and then the intersection itself becomes an **estimate generator**: every standard finite-order continuation estimate is obtained by projecting (\mathcal I[u_0]) onto a sufficiently high coordinate.

That is the core point.

### 1. Initial datum (\boldsymbol{u_0}) generates one history

Take

[
u_0\in H^\infty(\mathbb R^3)\cap L^2(\mathbb R^3),
\qquad
\nabla\cdot u_0=0,
\qquad
\nu>0.
]

Let ((u,p)) denote the maximal classical history generated by (u_0):

[
\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\nabla p
====================================

\nu\Delta u,
\qquad
\nabla\cdot u=0,
\qquad
u(0)=u_0.
\tag{1}
]

Incompressibility fixes pressure from the same velocity field:

[
-\Delta p
=========

\partial_i\partial_j(u_i u_j),
\qquad
p=R_iR_j(u_i u_j).
\tag{2}
]

So the proof carries one object:

[
\boxed{u_0\longrightarrow (u,p).}
]

### Serrin estimates

One standard continuation route asks for

[
u\in L_t^qL_x^p,
\qquad
\frac2q+\frac3p\le1,
\qquad
p>3.
]

Take the very simple row

[
u\in L^2(0,T_*;H^2).
]

Since

[
H^2(\mathbb R^3)\hookrightarrow L^\infty,
]

we obtain

[
\boxed{
u\in L^2(0,T_*;L^\infty).
}
\tag{17}
]

And

[
\frac22+\frac3\infty=1.
]

So one single finite intersection row already satisfies Serrin.

The master estimate (12) supplies the whole admissible Serrin family.

---

### Pressure estimates

Pressure is

[
p
=

R_iR_j(u_i u_j).
]

For every finite temporal order,

[
\partial_t^r p
==============

R_iR_j
\sum_{a=0}^r
\binom ra
(\partial_t^a u_i)
(\partial_t^{r-a}u_j).
\tag{25}
]

Since sufficiently high (H^m) spaces are algebras and the Riesz transforms are bounded,

[
\boxed{
\partial_t^r p
\in
C([0,T_*];H^m)
}
\tag{26}
]

for every finite (r,m), using a finite derivative margin.

Hence, for example,

[
\boxed{
\nabla p
\in
L^1(0,T_*;L^\infty).
}
\tag{27}
]

So pressure-based regularity criteria are also projections of the same intersection.

---

## 6. The intersection gives the endpoint itself

The zeroth temporal projection of the intersection gives

[
u
\in
\bigcap_{m<\infty}
L^2(0,T_*;H^m).
\tag{31}
]

For every finite (m),

[
|\mathbb P\nabla\cdot(u\otimes u)|*{H^m}
\le
C_m
|u|*{H^{m+2}}^2.
\tag{32}
]

Since

[
u\in L^2_tH_x^{m+2},
]

the nonlinear term belongs to (L^1_tH_x^m). Also

[
\Delta u\in L^1_tH_x^m.
]

From

[
u_t
===

## \nu\Delta u

\mathbb P\nabla\cdot(u\otimes u),
]

we get

[
u_t\in L^1(0,T_*;H^m).
]

Hence

[
u\in
W^{1,1}(0,T_*;H^m)
\hookrightarrow
C([0,T_*];H^m).
\tag{33}
]

This works for every finite (m). The endpoint values all come from the same velocity field, so they define one common endpoint

[
\boxed{
u_*
===

u(T_*)
\in
\bigcap_{m<\infty}H^m
=====================

H^\infty.
}
\tag{34}
]

That is stronger than any single classical continuation estimate.

---

## 7. The original equation generates the complete endpoint jet

Starting from

[
V_0(T_*)=u_*,
]

pressure gives

[
Q_0(T_*)
========

R_iR_j(u_{*,i}u_{*,j}),
]

then

[
V_1(T_*)
========

## \nu\Delta u_*

## (u_*\cdot\nabla)u_*

\nabla Q_0(T_*).
]

Since (u_*\in H^\infty),

[
V_1(T_*)\in H^\infty.
]

Repeat (3)–(4):

[
\boxed{
V_n(T_*),Q_n(T_*)
\in
H^\infty
\qquad
\forall n<\infty.
}
\tag{35}
]

Thus the alleged terminal point possesses the complete smooth pressure-compatible jet.

---
